Balake, d’un camp de réfugiés en Tanzani: Balake, from a refugee camp in Tanzania to the Université du Québec à Montréal
Balake a 22 ans. Né dans un camp de réfu: Balake is 22. Born in a refugee camp in Tanzania after his parents fled the war in Congo, he is now a student in Montréal.
Balake est un étudiant de 22 ans de l’UQ: Balake is a 22-year-old UQAM student. He has been in Quebec for 10 months, having left Tanzania through the World University Service of Canada’s Student Refugee Program. (Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy)
<strong>Balake a 22 ans. Né dans un camp: Balake is 22. Born in a refugee camp in Tanzania after his parents fled the war in Congo, he is now a student at the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM). His journey is one of determination and resilience, that of a young man guided by a dream: becoming a doctor. A profile.
Le hall du pavillon J.-A.-Desève de l’UQ: The lobby of UQAM’s J.-A.-DeSève Pavilion is quiet at the end of the semester. At the back, seated at a table, Balake gazes at the skyscrapers rising behind the huge bay window. Despite his shy nature, he agreed to share his story with La Converse. “In the camp where I grew up, a lot of young people think the student refugee programs aren’t real. I want them to know it’s true, that I’m here today and that they have hope of leaving the camp,” he says.
« Je suis au Québec depuis presque 10 mo: “I’ve been in Quebec for almost 10 months.” Balake counts in months, the way we do with babies, so much does his recent arrival feel like a rebirth. He himself didn’t believe it right away. It was, after all, a long and gruelling process, lasting several years, that finally put him among the few lucky ones selected by the World University Service of Canada (WUSC) Student Refugee Program (SRP).
Le PÉR est un programme qui offre à de j: The SRP is a program that gives young refugees the opportunity to pursue post-secondary studies in Canada. Thanks to agreements between the federal government and the Quebec government, sponsored students are welcomed as permanent residents. “I didn’t take it seriously because I thought it was impossible! A refugee coming to study in Canada, it seemed impossible to me,” Balake says with a shrug. “But then, the brother of someone I knew left through the program. That’s when I realized it was true.”
À l’UQAM, le comité bénévole de l’EUMC-P: At UQAM, the WUSC-SRP volunteer committee is made up of students who support two young people like Balake by providing, for one year: coverage of tuition fees, a room in student residence and a monthly stipend of $700 to meet their needs.
Pour atteindre son rêve, Balake a donc l: To reach his dream, Balake left behind his parents, his six sisters, his brother, his friends, and everything he had known until then in the refugee camp where he was born.
Depuis le milieu des années 1990, le Con: Since the mid-1990s, Congo has been mired in a conflict involving several local and foreign armed groups, as well as Congolese government forces and endemic intercommunal violence. The main cause of the conflict is the extraction of mineral resources in the east of the country, notably by Uganda and above all Rwanda.
« Le pays compte près de 7 millions de p: “The country has nearly 7 million displaced people, the highest number ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and one of the largest internal displacement crises in the world,” states a report by the Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, mandated by the UN Security Council and published in December 2023. The UNHCR, the United Nations refugee agency, also estimates that more than 8 67000 refugees and asylum seekers have found refuge in neighbouring countries. Among them, 8 8840 people were in Tanzania in September 2023.
Répartition des réfugiés et demandeurs d: Breakdown of refugees and asylum seekers who fled Congo by country of refuge in the region, according to September 2023 figures. (Infographic: UNHCR DIMA-RBSA)
Derrière la froideur des chiffres se tro: Behind the coldness of the numbers is Balake’s family, and so many others. “My parents are Congolese. They fled the war in 1996 and the Tanzanian government placed them in a refugee camp in the Kigoma region, in the east of the country. I was born and lived my whole life in that camp. Life was hard, but what’s cool is that I was surrounded by my family, my childhood friends…” says Balake, who never loses his mischievous smile.
Pourtant, ce camp au sein duquel sa mère: Yet the camp where his mother gave birth to him is none other than Nyarugusu. It is one of the largest refugee camps in the world. Created in 1996 to house 50,000 Congolese refugees, it is now home to nearly 14,000 people who fled Congo or Burundi. So what does daily life look like in such a setting? It was only after several hours that Balake finally agreed to share a few details.
« Le camp est composé de plusieurs petit: “The camp is made up of several small villages. At the beginning, when my parents arrived, they lived in tents, then they got organized over the years and things evolved a bit. I lived in a small one-room house with mud walls and a thatched roof. Others who arrived more recently were living in tents in 201,” Balake describes. He doesn’t complain. Never. He simply tells it as it is.
« C’est entouré de grilles avec plein de: “It’s surrounded by fences, with lots of police who stop people from leaving the camp. You can’t go work in town, for example. Leaving is only allowed in exceptional cases, for an illness or a death, and even then! So for food, the UNHCR distributes food every month. We get cornmeal, small loaves of bread, oil, salt and soy. But you can’t live on that for a month, so everyone figures it out by growing vegetables, raising sheep to sell at the market, or working to buy at the market, when there’s work.”
Sur son téléphone, Balake me montre des: On his phone, Balake shows me photos of his childhood. I discover the little boy he was, and I immediately recognize his inimitable smile. Barefoot on the ochre earth of this region of Tanzania, he is surrounded by two of his sisters. Beside them, women prepare a meal in front of a house made of mud and straw. A few photos later, I now see a teenager proudly posing with his childhood friend, plastic sandals on his feet, a soccer jersey on his back and a trendy haircut. “My hair was better back then, you see! Here it’s too expensive to get a haircut, so I’m letting it grow for now. My friend, he’s in the United States now, we call each other often,” says Balake.
De cette époque, il ne semble garder que: From that time, he seems to keep only the good memories. But above all, he finds in it the motivation to carve out a place and a better life for himself here.
Sa richesse, Balake la puise dans l’éduc: Balake draws his wealth from education. “My parents were elementary school principals in the camp, almost for free, of course. They made a lot of effort so that I could study, even if it wasn’t in the same conditions as they had at my age. We didn’t have a real school like here, we didn’t have the necessary materials, but still, I was able to study,” says the soccer enthusiast.
« La chose que je retiens et que mes par: “What I remember, and what my parents told me, is that school is like a path. If you’re passionate, if you persevere and you know what you’re going to do in life, you can go very far. They gave me lots of examples of people who became great figures thanks to their studies. That really stayed with me… A lot of young people weren’t studying back then, and it wasn’t easy for me to be different. I always had dreams and ambition, so I focused on that so I wouldn’t end up like other young people who drink traditional alcohol,” he says with emotion.
Isolés de tout, sans perspective d’aveni: Isolated from everything, with no prospect of a professional future, young refugees like Balake often have little hope of escaping the camp where their families sometimes have lived for several decades. Those who arrived more recently also carry the scars of the many traumas they faced in their countries and during their flight. All these ingredients lead many of them toward various addictions or violent behaviour. Balake was lucky to have parents who had been to school and who kept fanning the meagre embers of hope that remained, so that they would live on in their children’s hearts.
« Lorsque je suis né, j'ai passé presque: “When I was born, I spent almost three years in the hospital because I had breathing problems. I suffered a lot in my childhood,” Balake says softly. “The hospital was poorly equipped, and mothers died in childbirth, newborns died too. There weren’t enough doctors or medicine. In fact, after my birth, my mother lost two babies, two brothers, when I was five and eight years old. That’s why I want to become a doctor, to help all those refugees who are dying around the world for lack of care,” he murmurs as memories come back in fragments.
Il n’y a pas d’université à Nyarugusu. A: There is no university in Nyarugusu. After the equivalent of high school, Balake turned to veterinary technology, since he couldn’t study medicine. He studied for four years and worked for six months with farmers. But he never lost sight of his dream.

Seul luxe du foyer, la télévision est sa: The household’s only luxury, the television, was his window onto the outside world. “I wasn’t a big, big fan of movies, even if I watched some sometimes. I preferred watching the news from other countries. That’s how I saw how people lived elsewhere. And it was very, very different from the camp, because I didn’t have freedom,” he says. In 2020, his father told him about the student refugee program. The beginning of a long road to freedom.
Pendant un an, Balake s’est préparé aux: For a year, Balake prepared for the various selection stages to gain access to this exceptional opportunity. “In the first phase, there were 300 of us young people applying. They kept 80 to take the first French language test. After the test, I was among the 25 selected for the third phase, which is an interview where they ask about our motivations. And in the end I was among the last 10 selected to go to Canada,” he recalls with a glint of pride in his eyes.
En 2021, Balake reçoit le saint Graal :: In 2021, Balake received the Holy Grail: the official acceptance letter for a September 2022 start. Unfortunately, when it was time to leave in 2022, he got bad news. “They told us there wasn’t enough room in the universities for all ten selected. And since the program is only open to people under 25, they gave priority to the older ones. I was young, I was 20, so they pushed my scholarship to 2023,” Balake explains without any bitterness. He would wait one more year, patiently.
C’est finalement en août 2023, trois ans: It was finally in August 2023, three years after starting the process, that Balake left the Nyarugusu camp and Tanzania for the very first time in his life, bound for Montréal! A journey between two very different worlds. “When I arrived in Montréal, wow, it was wow,” he says, seeming at a loss for words. “I was passionate about Canada, I had done a lot of research, watched a lot of videos, but seeing it in real life was a shock,” says the young man, who appreciates architecture.
<strong>Le choc d’une nouvelle vie si di: The shock of a very different new life
Accueilli par des bénévoles engagés, Bal: Welcomed by dedicated volunteers, Balake discovered the lights, sounds and smells of the city he had fantasized about so much. A room was made available to him in the nearby student residence. But the euphoria soon gave way to the reality of daily life so far from home. “The hardest thing for me was leaving my family and living alone when I had spent my whole life surrounded by people. I felt very, very alone. And I was worried about my parents, because I helped them a lot with their tasks, especially with my mother, who has been sick for several years,” the young man confides.
L’étudiant peut compter sur les autres j: The student can count on the other young refugees from the Nyarugusu camp. “Some are in Ottawa, others in Quebec City, in Toronto and here, in Montréal. We have a close group and we support each other, because it’s true that it’s not easy to make friends. For now I’ve mostly built connections with international students! We play soccer together,” he says.
S’il est parvenu malgré tout à prendre s: Although he has managed to find his footing at university and in the city, Balake admits defeat when it comes to winter! “Oh là là, winter is too much! I couldn’t wait to see snow for the first time in my life, but the cold, honestly, I couldn’t do it,” he laughs. “I stayed in my room the whole time, I was really too cold. But next year I’m going to try skating.” Thanks to the student committee, he also takes part in activities organized regularly to introduce refugee students to Quebec culture.
But for him, that’s not what matters most. “This year I did a French certificate. I have one last exam and that’s it. After that, I’ll enrol in CEGEP in biology for the fall semester, and prepare for the medical school entrance exams, because it’s very, very difficult. In the meantime, I’m going to travel a bit, maybe to Quebec City to visit my friends I haven’t seen in a long time,” Balake says.
Concernant son futur, sans l’aide du PÉR: As for his future without the help of the SRP, whose support is set to end in August even though the volunteers will keep a personal connection with him, the twenty-something holds on to the optimism that defines him. With a determined look, he says: “I believe everything will go well if I give it my all and work hard. In life, hard work pays off.”
Balake est d’autant plus serein que sa f: Balake is all the more at ease because his family has, in turn, found refuge in the United States. “I’m so relieved since I found out they’ve been safe for three months. I would have preferred that they come here, because they speak French, so it would have been easier for them, but it’s not that far and they found work in restaurants. I’m very proud,” he says quietly.
L’année prochaine, le comité EUMC-PÉR de: Next year, UQAM’s WUSC-SRP committee hopes to welcome three new refugee students, one more than this year. None will come from the Nyarugusu camp. “We don’t know why, but the program was stopped there,” laments the young man, who knows just how much it can change the destiny of young refugees with no prospects.
Une chose est sûre, quand il sera médeci: One thing is certain: when he becomes a doctor, Balake will help those who stayed behind. “I don’t know how yet, but I want to do something for health in Africa, even if I stay and live here,” he says, like a promise…
